extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and policymakers interested in political theory and the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: A political essay (pamphlet) arguing normative principles for constitutional government and criticizing the French Revolution; addresses how constitutions should be preserved, reformed, and who should govern. Intended as persuasive commentary for policymakers and the literate public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare and preserve ancient rights as inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: "to declare and enacted that all and singular the rights and liberties asserted and declared are the true ancient and indubitable rights and liberties of the people of this kingdom"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat liberties as an entailed inheritance derived from forefathers and transmissible to posterity; use declaration of ancient rights as a foundational act to preserve constitutional unity and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform institutions to the 'method of nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Political institutions should "preserve the method of nature" and mirror natural processes of transmission, improvement, and conservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By following nature (inheritance, gradual transmission), constitutions secure stability while allowing improvement; this is preferable to speculative innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve variety and opposing interests within the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should contain a "variety of parts corresponding with the various descriptions of which your community was happily composed" so that "action and counteraction" draw out harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity of parts and conflicting interests operate as checks on precipitate resolutions, force compromise, and naturally temper extremes; avoid eliminating these opposing elements when reforming institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform by repairing existing foundations rather than starting anew
rubrics_metrics.description: When restoring or reforming government, one "might have repaired those walls; you might have built on those old foundations" rather than acting "as if you had never been molded into civil society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use existing constitutional elements and traditions as the basis for reform to preserve practical advantages and continuity; radical rejection of past institutions risks instability and loss of accumulated safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper liberty with gravity and historical reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of freedom "leading in itself to misrule and excess, is tempered with an awful gravity" when liberties are seen as part of a liberal descent with pedigree and ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame liberty within traditions, ceremonies, and historical honors (portraits, records, titles) to procure reverence and prevent the excesses of unrestrained freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rash, speculative innovations driven by selfish temper
rubrics_metrics.description: A "spirit of innovation is generally the result of a selfish temper and confined views"; innovators "will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspicion of radical, novelty-seeking reforms: prioritize prudence and long-term interests over fashionable speculation; consider intergenerational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure representative bodies are composed of people with property, education, and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can secure steady and moderate conduct in assemblies but that they "should be respectably composed, in point of condition in life or permanent property, of education, and of such habits as enlarge and liberalize the understanding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elect or select representatives with permanent property, education, and social standing so they can judge and temper leaders; avoid assemblies dominated by those lacking these attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overrepresentation of narrow professional interests (esp. inferior lawyers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dangerous composition arises when a majority are "practitioners in the law... of the inferior, unlearned, mechanical, merely instrumental members of the profession" leading to chicane and litigious dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent professions that are narrow, vexatious, or primarily local-litigation-focused from dominating national legislative power; their habits and incentives can produce mischievous governance and attacks on stability of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must have practical experience and virtue, not merely theory
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly composed mostly of "men of theory" but with no "practical experience in the state" will follow absurd projects unless rare, extraordinary virtue appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate leadership with real-world experience and public virtue; theoretical talent alone is insufficient to guide major political reorganization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Followers must be capable judges, not merely actors
rubrics_metrics.description: To be led otherwise than blindly, "the followers must be qualified, if not for actors, at least for judges; they must also be judges of natural weight and authority."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the electorate or assembly-members have sufficient judgment and social weight to constrain leaders; a populace without judging capacity risks being manipulated into harmful projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain constitutional restraints and fundamental laws on assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies that "have no fundamental law, no strict convention, no respected usage to restrain it" can remake the constitution to suit their designs, leaving nothing to control them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain fundamental laws, respected usage, and conventions to restrain assemblies; checks and balances and established practices prevent arbitrary reconstruction of the state by transient majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should include landed and mixed interests, not only urban or professional classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer notes a lack "of what we call the natural landed interest of the country" in the French Third Estate, implying this absence harms stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure representation includes landed and varied social interests so that legislation accounts for property stability, agriculture, and the broader economy rather than narrow mercantile or professional gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware clergy or poor representatives who may have incentives to plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: A large proportion of country curates, "immersed in hopeless poverty," may regard property "with no other eye than that of envy" and join attempts at plunder for small dividends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select clergy or religious representatives who are independent of petty wants or ensure electoral mechanisms that reduce incentives to expropriate; poverty-driven representation can bias decisions against property security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leveling that confuses equality with abolishing natural order
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those who attempt to level, never equalize... The levelers... change and pervert the natural order of things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between social amelioration and radical leveling; policies aiming to eliminate natural distinctions of social function risk destabilizing the social edifice and replacing necessary hierarchies with unsound structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect distinctions among occupations when assigning public authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While "no honest employment was disgraceful," asserting that "all occupations were honorable" implies inappropriate elevation of certain trades to governance, which risks unfit rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that not all employments prepare individuals for governance; avoid granting ruling power to groups whose occupations do not cultivate the necessary attributes for public authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable property and institutions are necessary for commerce, revenue, and public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: When property is subverted, consequences follow: "commerce expiring; the revenue unpaid... a state not relieved; civil and military anarchy... national bankruptcy" and discredited paper securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve property rights and conventional credit mechanisms to maintain commerce, revenue, public credit, and social order; undermining property leads to economic collapse and social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer leaders with long views and public spirit over mere usurpers
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary figures can differ: some (Cromwell, Richelieu, Henry IV, Sully) combined ambition with the aim to "illuminate and beautify the world," whereas others merely usurp and plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value leaders who pursue public good and long-term statecraft even if ambitious; leadership that seeks to elevate the state differs qualitatively from self-serving demagogues who destroy institutions for private gain.
